quotes.quote:
Artificial general intelligence (AGI) requires a method that can understand, generate, reason, and act across diverse domains and modalities.
Rather than relying on a single model to master every capability, a promising path toward AGI now is to orchestrate a heterogeneous ecosystem of specialized models, tools, and policies (candidates) into a unified AI system.
At the heart of this vision lies a fundamental question: how can an AI system dynamically select and coordinate the most capable candidate for each task while balancing performance and computational cost?
In this work, we present Route Anything, a unified framework for studying model and policy routing across general-purpose AI systems.
We develop a unified theoretical foundation that characterizes optimal routing under quality–cost trade-offs and establishes how the information available to a router determines its attainable performance.
To systematically investigate routing across diverse capabilities, we first construct an omni-modal trajectory matrix spanning 25 benchmarks across language understanding, image, video, and speech generation, coding and workplace agents, and robotic manipulation, comprising 374,401 scored runs from 452 candidate configurations.
Building on this framework, we train and test different routers to investigate the potential of omni-modal model routing, the capabilities of learned routers, and the conditions under which routing improves efficiency.
Our results reveal substantial opportunities for capability orchestration: per-input oracle routing outperforms the best fixed candidate by 5.4 points, and learned routers outperform it by 0.3 points across 16 benchmarks, by 2.1 points on video generation, and by 1.1 points on robot manipulation while using 24% less policy time. More importantly, routing raises efficiency by 8.82 × 8.82\times on average compared with the reference model, including 25.5 × 25.5\times on coding tasks and 7.1 × 7.1\times on text question answering.

Routing research has mostly studied language models: cascades that escalate to a stronger model [ 1 ] , routers learned from preferences [ 2 ] , and quality–cost formulations that connect the two [ 3 ] . Whether routing helps across modalities remains an open question. Thus we present a unified framework Route Anything for studying model and policy routing across modalities. To support such anlyasitical framework, we first build an omni-modal trajectory matrix in which every candidate in a pool runs on the same inputs, for 25 benchmarks across text and image understanding, image, video, and speech generation, code and workplace agents, and robot manipulation, with three to seven candidates per pool and 374,401 scored runs of 452 candidate configurations (Figure 1 ). We train and test routers using different strategies and ask three questions: how much can routing gain, how well do learned routers work, and when is a cheaper route good enough?

(1) A unified theory of routing. We connect resource prices and quality constraints to optimal model and policy selection, and characterize how the information available to a router determines its attainable performance (§ 2 ). (2) An omni-modal trajectory matrix. We run 452 candidate configurations on the same inputs of 25 benchmarks across text and image understanding, image, video, and speech generation, code and workplace agents, and robot manipulation, for 374,401 scored runs (§ 3 and Appendix B ). (3) The potential of omni-modal routing. We quantify the potential gain of routing (5.4 points over the best fixed candidate), train and test learned routers that beat the best fixed candidate by 0.3 points overall and 2.1 points on video generation, show that task-type labels capture 8% of the potential gain on benchmarks with such labels, and examine how training targets and baseline choices affect measured gains (§ 3 and § 4 ). (4) When routing improves efficiency. We show that routing raises efficiency over the reference by 8.82 × 8.82\times on average and up to 25.5 × 25.5\times on code with matched quality, and evaluate on diverse conditions (§ 5 ).

This semi-synthetic study combines real outputs and verifier judgments with constructed arrivals and retention: 2,044 probing and 867 test tasks in 12 cells. With probability 0.25 the writer explores a uniformly sampled model, and it writes the model’s identity to the arriving cell when verification accepts; the newest record serves later tasks in that cell, and uncovered cells use the prior, always-Opus or the probing-fitted DimensionBest, which sends each dimension to its best model. Writers use ACRouter’s doctest and syntax tools, locally executed hidden tests, or a DeepSeek-v4-pro judge; we report hidden-test writes. A write is erroneous when the accepted output is incorrect under the released score; against that truth, hidden-test writes have TPR/FPR 0.960/0.205. Fifty streams of 60,000 rounds are measured over their last 10,000 rounds. With no expiration, the store reaches 135.8 score per dollar but scores 0.034 below always-Opus and 0.116 below DimensionBest.

quotes.quote: Speculative decoding accelerates memory-bound LLM decoding with a lightweight drafter, and parallel drafters extend this speedup by drafting a whole block in one forward pass. However, it remains unclear whether their released systems ( stock ) attain the full speedup that parallel drafting permits. We identify three challenges. First, with one request, each step accepts few tokens but reads every target weight. Second, with batching, per-request verification work roughly halves the speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding. Third, speculative decoding is deployment-specific, and no universal optimization fits every serving regime, drafter, target model and GPU. To address these challenges, we present SpecPilot, an autonomous agentic loop that discovers algorithms and systems optimizations for each deployment. In each round, a cost model locates the largest gaps between the current system and its ceiling. Parallel agents explore directions and integrate the successful ones. Token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect reward hacking. A structured memory carries validated mechanisms to new rounds and deployments. SpecPilot discovered a general lossless 12-bit weight format, tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three batching mechanisms. We evaluate it across four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stock’s 4.46 × \times to 10.87 × \times with one request, and from 1.94 × \times to 3.93 × \times with batching.

We present SpecPilot (Figure 3 ), an autonomous agentic loop that searches for speculative decoding optimizations tailored to each deployment. It rests on four ideas. First, a cost model compares measured performance with an estimated ceiling to locate where speed is lost. Second, parallel agents explore multiple directions on separate GPUs and integrate the validated pieces, so small gains add up. Third, a controller isolated from the agents accepts a change only on a significant gain confirmed on unseen requests, and token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect lossy changes (§ 3.3 ). Finally, validated optimizations are distilled into a structured memory as replayable code and evidence, for reuse in later rounds and new deployments.

Discovered Lossless Algorithms: SpecPilot discovered W12, a general lossless 12-bit weight format, best-first tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three mechanisms for batching.

quotes.quote:
An agent harness comprises the prompts, tools, middleware, and control logic surrounding the underlying LLM ( Zhou et al., 2026 ) .
Let h ∈ ℋ h\in\mathcal{H} denote a candidate harness and m m the underlying LLM, which remains fixed throughout optimization. Executing the agent ( h , m ) (h,m) on task x x induces a stochastic trajectory τ ∼ p ⁡ ( τ ∣ h , m , x ) , \tau\sim p(\tau\mid h,m,x), with randomness arising from model generation and interactions with tools and the environment.

ParetoSaddler brings Pareto reasoning into the promotion decisions of staged
harness optimization. As illustrated in
Figure 2 , at iteration t t , the optimizer
selects a parent harness h t h_{t} and uses generation samples 𝒟 t gen ⊆ 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{t}^{\mathrm{gen}}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} to construct a candidate h t ′ h^{\prime}_{t} ( 1 ). These samples provide the execution traces and other
method-specific evidence used to derive the update. The parent and candidate are then assessed using screening samples 𝒟 t scr ⊆ 𝒟 train \mathcal{D}_{t}^{\mathrm{scr}}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} , which may differ from or overlap with the
generation samples.
During screening, the parent and candidate are repeatedly executed under a shared evaluation protocol, yielding joint quality–cost observations.

A statistical Pareto promotion rule ( 2 ) uses these observations to advance a candidate when there is sufficient evidence of improvement in either quality or cost, without requiring the update to satisfy a particular deployment preference. Promoted candidates then receive broader development evaluation ( 3 ), which updates the development-evaluated alternatives and their empirical Pareto archive. The resulting alternatives, together with the deployment preference π \pi , guide continued optimization ( 4 ), forming an iterative
loop. After the optimization budget is exhausted, the deployment preference π \pi is applied to the retained candidates to determine the returned harness or harness set ( 5 ). Algorithms 1 and 2 provide the general procedure and its AutoSaddler instantiation, respectively.

quotes.quote:
Abstract. Later tokens are costlier to generate than earlier tokens.
On frontier open weight models, the disparity in cost may rise to as much as 7x.
Through frequent compaction, we show across a broad range of long-horizon and long-input tasks that frontier language models sacrifice little to no task accuracy when maintaining short contexts.
We further demonstrate that LLM performance does not collapse on long-horizon software engineering tasks even when taking at most one action per context, and based on that we outline the concept of semantic state space models (SSSMs).
Our findings question the need for long-context language models.

Not all tokens are generated equal.
Token generation latency and memory footprint both grow with the number of tokens in a language model’s context.
This is due to the inherent linear 1 1 1 Model architectures with a constant cost of token generation with respect to context depth have been repeatedly proposed but have never been fully embraced – linear-cost attention-based mechanisms remain the backbone of all popular language models. relationship between the computational cost of generating a token and its depth within a context [ 25 ] . Figure 1 shows the cloud token generation cost as a function of context window size for a selection of popular open-weight models.
Observe that there is a considerable monetary benefit to serving models on cloud GPUs with consistently shorter contexts.
This fact is often hidden from the end user since retail token prices are quoted at a fixed price per 1 1 M tokens regardless of the input context length.
Note that the extent of cost reductions ( 3.6 × 3.6\times to 7 × 7\times ) rivals or exceeds that of many other orthogonal optimization methods such as aggressive quantization or structured sparsification [ 5 , 14 , 8 ] .

The context window is the space of tokens an LM can comprehend at any given point, usually imposed by the model’s architecture or indirectly by its post-training data bias.
Contexts exceeding context windows may cause system errors or unexpected behavior.
The context window size is the maximum number of tokens that an LM endpoint can process in one invocation, whether imposed by the model’s context window or narrowed by its serving configuration.

quotes.quote: Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.

We call this approach Adversarial Speculative Reasoning. We locate critical thinking in agent traces and build preference pairs between alternative decision framings. We then train the draft with direct preference optimization (DPO; Rafailov et al., 2023 ) in the reverse direction: the draft learns to prefer the framing the target should avoid. At inference, the draft and the target diverge precisely at these points, so the target’s own choice is committed through residual sampling and encoded precisely in the KV cache. The target model is unchanged, and so is the verification rule and its exactness guarantee. Only the draft model is changed and context precision is re-allocated. With this approach, we significantly improve long-horizon agent reasoning accuracy without hurting inference efficiency. For example, on DeepSWE Huang and Jiang (2026) , a benchmark of complex software-engineering tasks, Adversarial Speculative Reasoning raises the end-to-end success rate of GLM-5.3-nvfp4 from 60.6% to 67.6% (+7.0 points). It raises DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash from 67.8% to 71.8% (+4.0 points) with the standard evaluation harness and environments. Overall, we make the following contributions:

quotes.quote:
Evaluating a harness on 𝒟 v \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{v}} is costly, as each task may
require multiple model and tool calls. We therefore consider a sequential
optimization protocol initialized from a harness h 0 h_{0} and constrained by a
budget of N N refinement attempts. At each attempt, the optimizer draws on
accumulated validation scores and execution traces to select an existing
harness for refinement and propose a new candidate. The central challenge
is to allocate refinement
effort across alternative paths while further developing promising designs.
At the end of search, we select the harness with the highest observed score
on 𝒟 v \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{v}} among the candidates produced during
optimization. The selected harness is then evaluated on a
disjoint held-out test set 𝒟 t \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{t}} , and the resulting score
is reported as its final performance.

Each candidate is represented by a complete executable codebase. Refinement
may add, remove, or jointly modify mechanisms for context construction,
state management, control flow, and tool use. This allows a single proposal
to coordinate changes across interacting mechanisms, supporting both local
improvements and broader architectural changes within the search space
defined in Section 2 .

The coding agent develops each candidate from a selected parent harness,
guided by accumulated search experience. We denote the experience archive
by 𝒜 \mathcal{A} ; it contains prior implementations, code modifications,
validation feedback, task-level execution records, and refinement
relationships. The parent supplies the starting design, while the archive
provides empirical evidence about the effects of earlier changes. The agent
can selectively retrieve relevant code and feedback to compare designs,
diagnose failures, and identify refinements, without requiring the entire
search history to fit in its context.

After n n refinement attempts, the search retains evaluated candidates
in a rooted tree 𝒢 n = ( 𝒱 n , ℰ n ) \mathcal{G}_{n}=(\mathcal{V}_{n},\mathcal{E}_{n}) . Each node u i ∈ 𝒱 n u_{i}\in\mathcal{V}_{n} represents a harness h i h_{i} together with its validation
score q i q_{i} and execution records ℛ i \mathcal{R}_{i} ; the root u 0 u_{0} represents
the initial harness h 0 h_{0} . An edge ( u i , u j ) (u_{i},u_{j}) indicates that h j h_{j} was
generated by refining h i h_{i} . Each evaluated harness and its measured score
remain unchanged as the tree grows, preserving earlier designs and alternative
refinement paths. Expansion counts and accumulated experience evolve
with the search. HarnessFlow adapts the MCTS
cycle ( Browne et al., 2012 ) through selection, expansion, evaluation, and
experience backpropagation.

Each benchmark is split once with a fixed random seed ( 42 42 ) into a validation
set used during search and a disjoint test set used only for the final
evaluation: 92 92 / 186 186 tasks for TAU2-bench, 105 105 / 210 210 for AppWorld, and 100 100 / 200 200 for WebShop, BrowseComp-Plus, SWE-bench Verified, and
BigCodeBench-Hard, whose tasks are sampled from the BigCodeBench release
using its published difficulty criteria. The same split and the benchmark’s
official grader are used for every method.

Each search runs N = 15 N=15 candidate attempts, and every proposed candidate
consumes one attempt. In Algorithm 1 , v n v_{n} is valid when
the candidate passes a runtime compatibility check and its evaluation yields
a score. Selection uses the parameters given in Section 4.1 , and
every candidate, including the root, is scored on the validation split with R = 5 R=5 repetitions per task. Meta-Harness is run through the same pipeline
with the same initial harness, coding agent, and candidate budget.

quotes.quote: The outer loop was exercised on five human protein assays, one assay per ProteinGym functional category; the category label printed in each panel of Fig. 3 is given first in parentheses. Folding stability (Stability, OTU7A) predicts whether a single substitution causes the domain to unfold. Antibody binding (Binding, CD19) requires 3,761 variants to be ranked by whether they are still recognised by a monoclonal antibody. Expression of rhodopsin (Expression, OPSD) judges whether the protein reaches its correct location. Cell viability (Activity, NPC1) and channel function (Organismal fitness, SCN5A/Nav1.5) ask whether the protein still works in a cellular and in a whole-physiological context. The outer loop changes only how the harness is organised, which includes the inputs that are read, the order in which tools are called and the points at which checks are placed; it does not change model weights.

Three boundaries apply to what has been shown here. First, the outer-loop gain of 0.044 is measured on the development set, the set the harness was permitted to use during evolution; of the five endpoints ranked against the official record, only the CD19 first place was produced by the outer loop itself, while the expression first place derives from the tool combination already present at the starting point. Second, the ranking gap exposed on RLuc is named here as a trigger condition for the inner loop but has not yet been closed: the inner loop was exercised on a stability task and an extrapolation task, not against this gap, so whether method development can repair within-pool ranking remains open. Third, the three enzyme tests examine the system’s experimental decision-making rather than a complete dry-to-wet cycle driven by the two loops; the commission, execution and receipt path of Section 4.6 is specified but has not yet carried a multi-round campaign end to end, which we treat as a scope decision for this report rather than an unresolved capability.

From the trajectories of development tasks the outer loop identifies failure modes, which include incomplete parsing of the objective, a mismatched choice of tool, an inappropriate order of steps, evidence that the next step does not consume, and budget spent on ineffective repetition. For one failure mode it proposes one explicit hypothesis and one minimal consistent change bundle. The bundle records the parent version, the difference, the metric expected to improve, the falsification condition, the range of tasks to which it applies and the evaluation plan, which prevents post hoc explanation from replacing prior prediction; every item in a bundle can be disabled individually so that items can be ablated one at a time. The candidate version and the current version are compared in pairs under the same foundation model, tool permissions, visible data and budget. The outer loop may access development evidence only; the validation set is used solely for the stopping and version-selection rules agreed in advance, and the final test set takes no part in generating changes.

A version may replace the current version only when its products are valid, the primary metric meets the adoption condition set in advance, the key constraints are satisfied and the cost is acceptable. A candidate whose overall gain is insufficient but which gives a reproducible gain within a predefined task category is retained as a category-specific version. A task already in progress stays bound to the assets with which it started. An adoption event must update the version register and record which version the next run actually consumed: generating a candidate, or writing out a recommendation to adopt, does not by itself close the loop.

The evaluation contract of the outer loop. The outer loop was run on one assay from each of five classes of human protein measurement, for 196 rounds in total. The primary metric was spearman_macro with a minimum acceptable increment of 0.001. In each round the control version and the candidate version were compared in pairs on the same assay, for 142 comparisons in total.

The procedure of each round. Each round runs proposal, application, paired comparison under matched conditions, gating, and adoption or rollback, in that order. The assets that may be changed are limited to skills, MCP tool access, subagents and the system prompt; model weights and the scoring algorithm are unchanged throughout. Any change that fails the gate is rolled back to the parent commit, and the changed files and the commit identifier of every round are retained for traceability. The five endpoints were ranked alongside the 97 published models in the official per-assay ProteinGym record, taken from a frozen snapshot. To confirm that our endpoints and the official record were computed on the same basis, we recomputed the official Average Spearman with the same script and matched the official overall table item by item to three decimal places.

items.title: Reglos: A Self-Evolving Personal Memory Agent with Recursive Self-Improvement
items.reason_zh: 外层 coding agent 按失败轨迹修改记忆检索、过滤排序和上下文组织的程序，经独立critic与固定评测筛选；跨用户持续部署该程序。

evidence.extraction: BeautifulSoup article h2,h3,h4,p; zero-based block index

quotes.quote: We present Reglos , a training-free personal memory agent built on this principle (Figure 2 ). Its inner loop is a self-evolving memory. Each fact enters an append-only record that stores when it holds and when it was learned, so a new preference can supersede an old one without erasing it. A request to forget expires the matching facts, and a nightly pass rewrites the profile from the user’s current facts. Because these states are explicit, the harness can tell the model which of two conflicting preferences is current and what it must not use. Its outer loop improves the harness through recursive self-improvement. A coding agent reads failure traces and writes patches, and a critic from a second model family clusters the same failures and rejects patches that game the benchmark. After the harness is frozen, a fixed evaluator accepts a patch only if it helps users held out from development. The two loops co-evolve. The outer loop learns from the failures of the memory the inner loop builds, and each accepted patch changes how that memory is written and read. Qwen3.8-27B writes memory throughout.

In the sense of Duan et al. (2026) , recursive self-improvement (RSI) is an autonomous, closed loop whose changes persist and alter later improvement. One line of recent work trains the model inside that loop ( Lin et al. 2026 ; Zhang et al. 2026a ) . Another is training-free and evolves the harness around a frozen model ( Lee et al. 2026b ; Zhang et al. 2026c ; Lee et al. 2026a ) , and some systems combine the two ( Wei et al. 2026 ; Su et al. 2026 ) . RSI has also reached memory: MemPro, PrisMem and ALMA evolve the memory pipeline as code ( Liu et al. 2026b ; Chen et al. 2026 ; Xiong, Hu, and Clune 2026 ) , and D 2 ACCI gates memory changes with statistical tests ( Liu et al. 2026c ) . Reglos belongs to the training-free harness line, at the level of strategy autonomy: a coding agent proposes harness code, the task model stays frozen, and a fixed evaluator decides which changes to keep.

The harness is the program that sits between the memory kernel and the frozen task model and determines what the model reads. It receives the question, together with its answer options where the benchmark provides them, but has no access to the dataset’s labels. Memory is reachable only through a narrow interface: recall, the list of stored items, the user’s profile and the source messages of each fact. Within this interface the harness may issue several recall queries, filter and rank the results across memory layers, and decide how the evidence is organized. These decisions form the search space of the outer loop (Section 3.4 ).

We evolve the harness on PersonaMem-v2 ( Jiang et al. 2025b ) , whose four-way questions turn on implicit, revised or retracted preferences, on preferences that belong to someone else, and on information the user asked not to repeat. Qwen3.8-27B (reasoning off) writes memory and answers throughout. The loop sees only the validation split. We report all PersonaMem-v2 results on the official 5,000-question test set. We scored it once after the freeze and never read its failures (Appendix C ).

The proposer is the coding agent Claude Code ( Anthropic 2025 ) running Claude Opus 5.5. It reads raw failure traces and writes a patch to the harness, following the finding that raw traces carry more signal than summaries ( Lee et al. 2026b ) . The critic is Codex ( OpenAI 2025 ) running GPT-6.1 Sol, so the proposer and the critic come from different model families. The critic clusters the same failures independently and rejects any patch keyed to the dataset’s option templates or labels. A fixed evaluator then decides. After the freeze, every candidate faces the rule of Figure 4 : it must gain on each of two persona-disjoint validation halves (1,317 questions) and may cost a second reader at most one point; GPT-5.6 Luna is that reader and answers from the same contexts. Humans fix the objective, the splits and the rule; the proposer decides what to change. In the taxonomy of Duan et al. (2026) this is strategy autonomy (L2), and the inner loop is environment adaptation (L4); Appendix C maps both loops onto their components.

After the engine patch, four accepted steps took the harness from 54.2% to 60.7% on the 1,317 validation questions, overtaking the full history given the same policy (55.0%) at its first step (Figure 6 ). Table 5 lists the steps; the largest single gain came from a revised policy that treats memory as incomplete and keeps sensitive identifiers private. The final harness carries over to the held-out benchmark split, where the same model rises from 49.3% reading the full history to 61.3% (Table 1 ).

Writing one persona’s 32k-token history to memory costs about 225k to 260k task-model tokens (roughly 7.5 times the history) and 40k embedding tokens, amortized over 25 questions per persona. Answering costs about 6.0k prompt tokens per question, so judging one candidate on 1,317 questions with two readers takes about 16M prompt tokens. Writing memory for the 200 test personas took about 50M task-model tokens and six hours at eight-way concurrency.

During development a change was kept when it did not lower accuracy on the tuning slices, and it replaced the current harness once it gained about 3 points. This margin proved close to run-to-run noise, so after the freeze we adopted the stricter rule of Figure 4 , with GPT-5.6 Luna as the second reader.

items.title: EvoGuard: Mitigating Degradation in Online Skill Evolution
items.reason_zh: 每项任务后按轨迹重写可复用技能，固定selector选择是否替换，下一任务继续消费同family技能；在线executor/generator/selector都不训练。

quotes.quote: To address these gaps, we propose EvoGuard , a pairwise skill selector that amortizes validation. Tasks are grouped into task families, and each family keeps one skill. After each task, a fixed generator writes a new skill from the latest trajectory. EvoGuard then decides whether this new skill replaces the current skill. This decision only requires the relative order of the two skills, not their absolute utilities. We therefore cast it as a pairwise preference problem. We pay the cost of validation once before deployment and use it to train the selector. After that, each decision only compares two skill texts.

EvoGuard works in three stages (Figure 2 ). (1) Multi-source skill pool construction. We run the rewrite loop on training tasks with a base generator and an expert generator, and collect the generated skills into a pool. (2) Utility-grounded pairwise preference learning. We estimate the utility of every skill on a private test set of its family. Rejection sampling keeps pairs from the same family with a clear utility gap. We then train a pairwise selector to predict which skill in a pair has the higher utility. (3) Online skill selection. After every task, the frozen selector reads the family description and the two skills. It keeps the skill it predicts to be better. This takes one forward pass and runs no extra rollouts in the environment.

Skills package reusable experience as executable code or structured documents ( Wang et al., 2024a ; Anthropic, 2025 ; Xu and Yan, 2026 ) . Recent work evolves skills from interaction. SkillRL integrates recursive skill evolution with reinforcement learning ( Xia et al., 2026 ) . SkillOpt treats a skill as the external state of a frozen agent and optimizes it under feedback ( Yang et al., 2026b ) . SkillRise is the closest work to ours ( Yao et al., 2026 ) . It also carries an evolving skill across distinct tasks and trains the executor jointly with skill curation through reinforcement learning. However, our method keeps both the executor and the generator frozen. It only decides whether a single-trajectory rewrite should replace the current skill. This decision is learned from supervised pairwise labels without policy optimization. EvoGuard is thus a separate module that can be attached to any rewrite loop.

Tasks arrive one at a time. Let ℱ \mathcal{F} be the set of task families. The t t -th task is x t x_{t} , and its family is f t ∈ ℱ f_{t}\in\mathcal{F} . Each family f f keeps one textual skill s f s_{f} . Every skill starts as the empty document ∅ \varnothing . A frozen executor E E attempts x t x_{t} with the current skill s f t s_{f_{t}} . It returns a trajectory τ t \tau_{t} and an outcome r t r_{t} that measures task success:

The executor observes the current task and the environment feedback. The generator observes the current skill, the latest trajectory, and its outcome. The selector observes only the family name, a generic family description, and the two skill texts. It does not see the latest task, its trajectory, or its outcome.

For each family f f , we split the training tasks into two parts. A small part serves as the private test set ℋ f \mathcal{H}_{f} . The other part is used to build the skill pool 𝒫 f \mathcal{P}_{f} . The pool is filled by the rewrite loop itself. The first few tasks run without a skill, and their valid rewrites initialize the pool. For every later task x x , we draw a parent skill s s uniformly from the pool. The executor attempts x x with s s and returns ( τ , r ) = E ⁡ ( x , s ) (\tau,r)=E(x,s) . The generator then rewrites s s . The new skill joins the pool if it passes the format check:

At deployment every family starts from the empty skill. Consider a task of family f f whose rewrite s ~ \tilde{s} passes the format check. We place the current skill s f s_{f} and s ~ \tilde{s} at positions A and B in random order, as in training. The selector is then queried once. It returns the position with the larger logit. The skill at that position becomes the family skill:

This rule implements the selector C C in Eq. ( 3 ). The prompt is the same as in training. One decision costs one forward pass. It generates no tokens and runs no extra rollouts. Neither the selector nor the executor is updated online. Appendix A.2 gives the prompts, Appendix A.4 describes how the selector is served, and Appendix A.5 gives the full online loop.

We evaluate on four benchmarks and use their test sets for online evaluation. ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2021 ) is a text-based household environment. An agent completes tasks such as finding, heating, or cleaning objects through text commands. Its tasks fall into six families, namely Pick, Look, Clean, Heat, Cool, and Pick2. We use its seen and unseen test splits with 140 and 134 tasks. ScienceWorld ( Wang et al., 2022 ) is a text-based environment for elementary science experiments. Each of its 30 task types forms a family. We draw at most 30 test tasks per type, which gives 651 test tasks. LiveCodeBench ( Jain et al., 2025 ) collects competitive programming problems over time. We use the 175 problems added in its sixth release as the test set. Codex with GPT-6.1-sol assigns each problem to one of nine algorithmic categories (Appendix A.1 ). These categories serve as families. WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) simulates online shopping. An agent searches a store and buys a product that matches an instruction. Its five product categories serve as families, and we use its 500 test tasks.

Our experiments cover text-based agent environments and one code generation benchmark. Extending EvoGuard to multimodal or embodied settings is left for future work. All executors come from one model family. Other model families may rank skills somewhat differently. Building and scoring the skill pool requires offline computation before deployment. This cost is paid once and is shared by all later decisions. We train one selector per benchmark. A single selector that transfers across domains would further reduce the setup cost. The selector compares the current skill with one new skill at a time. Richer update rules, such as keeping several versions or reverting to an earlier one, may bring further gains. Finally, the selector can only choose among the rewrites it receives. Its benefit is therefore smaller in settings where skills offer little help.

测试期间存在在线技能更新，不能表述为冻结Harness的独立留出评测；结论不可泛化为所有任务族外迁移。
